title: Taxonomy basics
description: A taxonomy is a hierarchy of concepts — animal -> mammal -> dog — where each level inherits the properties of its parents. Building one means choosing the dimensions (by function? by material?), keeping siblings mutually exclusive, and deciding depth (5-7 levels is the practical max before navigation collapses). Good taxonomies feel inevitable; bad ones feel like someone's org chart.
mechanism: Top-down (define levels, populate) or bottom-up (cluster instances, name the clusters). Rules: single inheritance for the primary axis, siblings exclusive, depth bounded. Polyhierarchy (multiple parents) where reality demands it.
algo: O(concepts) to build; the design is human. Navigation is O(depth).

title: Hypernyms and hyponyms
description: Hypernym/hyponym is the IS-A relation: 'dog' is a hyponym of 'mammal', 'mammal' the hypernym of 'dog'. Mining these relations from text uses Hearst patterns ('X such as Y', 'Y and other X') — simple, high-precision, and still the baseline every fancy method beats. WordNet encodes millions of these links for English; every language needs its own.
mechanism: Hearst patterns over parsed text: 'mammals such as dogs' -> (dog, IS-A, mammal). Validate with distributional checks (hyponym contexts are narrower). Store in the taxonomy/knowledge graph.
algo: O(sentences) pattern matching; precision high, recall modest — the baseline.

title: Synonym expansion
description: Synonym expansion grows queries with equivalent terms: 'car' also searches 'automobile', 'vehicle'. Sources: WordNet synsets, distributional similarity (words in similar contexts), and click logs ('users searching X clicked Y'). The risk is drift — 'apple' the fruit vs the company — so expansion is weighted and context-gated, never a blind OR of everything.
mechanism: Synset lookup + distributional candidates; weight by similarity; gate by query context (disambiguate first). Expand at query time with weights, or at index time (bigger index, faster queries).
demo:
# weighted, context-gated expansion (not a blind OR)
SYN = {
    'car': [('automobile', 0.9), ('vehicle', 0.7)],
    'apple': [('fruit', 0.5), ('Apple Inc.', 0.5)],  # ambiguous!
}

def expand(term, context=''):
    cands = SYN.get(term, [])
    if term == 'apple':  # disambiguate by context first
        cands = [c for c in cands if ('Inc' in c[0]) == ('stock' in context or 'iphone' in context)]
    return [(term, 1.0)] + cands

print('car  :', expand('car'))
print('apple ("iphone review"):', expand('apple', 'iphone review'))
print('apple ("pie recipe")   :', expand('apple', 'pie recipe'))

title: Knowledge graphs
description: Knowledge graphs store facts as (subject, predicate, object) triples — (Ada, invented, Analytical Engine) — forming a queryable web of entities and relations. They power semantic search, recommendations, and question answering: multi-hop queries ('students of Ada's collaborators') are graph traversals. Construction mixes extraction (from text), curation (humans), and imports (Wikidata).
mechanism: Triples in a graph DB; SPARQL/Cypher for queries; entity linking to canonicalize mentions; inference over ontological relations (transitivity of IS-A). Quality from provenance per triple.
algo: Multi-hop queries are graph traversals O(branching^hops); indexes on (s,p,o) permutations.
demo:
# triples + multi-hop query: students of Ada's collaborators
triples = [
    ('Ada', 'collaborated_with', 'Babbage'),
    ('Babbage', 'mentored', 'Henry'),
    ('Ada', 'mentored', 'Willy'),
]

def query(s, p, o=None):
    return [t for t in triples if (s is None or t[0] == s) and t[1] == p and (o is None or t[2] == o)]

collabs = [t[2] for t in query('Ada', 'collaborated_with')]
students = [t[2] for c in collabs for t in query(c, 'mentored')]
print('Ada collaborated with:', collabs)
print('their students:', students, '(2-hop traversal)')

title: Query expansion with ontologies
description: Ontologies expand queries along their relations: searching 'mammal' also matches 'dog' and 'cat' (hyponyms), and searching 'dog' can broaden to 'mammal' when recall is low. The expansion follows the graph — synonyms, hypernyms, meronyms (part-of) — with weights decaying by distance. It turns a vocabulary mismatch ('user says pup, docs say dog') into a match.
mechanism: At query time: traverse the ontology from query terms up to N hops; add related terms with decayed weights; run the expanded query. Control with expansion depth and per-relation weights.

title: Concept drift
description: Concepts drift: 'phone' meant a wall device in 1990 and a computer in 2020; new senses appear ('cloud'), old ones fade. Ontologies must version senses with time intervals and track the drift — otherwise historical queries misinterpret ('phone records from 1985' are not iPhones). Detection mines time-stamped corpora for shifting word contexts.
mechanism: Time-sliced embeddings; sense inventory per time period; drift = distance between a word's embeddings across periods. Version the ontology: senses carry valid intervals.
algo: O(periods * vocab) embedding comparison. Versioning is the engineering response.

title: Embedding-based expansion
description: Distributional semantics finds related terms without hand-built taxonomies: words appearing in similar contexts get similar vectors, and nearest neighbors are expansion candidates. It discovers relations the curators missed ('vector DB' ~ 'embedding store') and works for any domain with enough text. The catch is the relations are unlabeled — similar, not synonymous — so weights stay modest and context gates stay on.
mechanism: Train embeddings on domain text; nearest neighbors per query term are candidates; weight by cosine; gate by the query's other terms. Combine with the curated ontology (curated first, distributional second).
algo: O(vocab) training; O(1) ANN lookup per term at query time.

title: Faceted ontologies
description: Faceted ontologies organize by independent dimensions — a laptop is (brand: X, RAM: 16GB, use: gaming) — instead of one hierarchy. Facets compose: users filter by combining them, and the ontology stays shallow because dimensions multiply instead of nesting. E-commerce runs on facets; the design work is choosing orthogonal dimensions and keeping their values clean.
mechanism: Define facets (orthogonal dimensions) with value vocabularies; classify items per facet; query = facet conjunctions. Values curated per facet; hierarchies within a facet allowed (gaming -> esports).
algo: O(facets) per classification; queries are conjunctions over facet indexes.
demo:
# facets: independent dimensions, composed at query time
items = [
    {'name': 'X1', 'brand': 'A', 'ram': 16, 'use': 'gaming'},
    {'name': 'Y2', 'brand': 'B', 'ram': 16, 'use': 'office'},
    {'name': 'Z3', 'brand': 'A', 'ram': 32, 'use': 'gaming'},
]

def search(**facets):
    return [i['name'] for i in items if all(i[k] == v for k, v in facets.items())]

print('ram=16:', search(ram=16))
print('brand=A + use=gaming:', search(brand='A', use='gaming'))
print('dimensions multiply instead of nesting: the ontology stays shallow')

title: Ontology versioning
description: Ontologies change — concepts added, merged, split, deprecated — and downstream indexes must track which version they were built with. Versioning means immutable releases with changelogs, deprecation (not deletion) of concepts, and migration maps (old concept -> new). Queries declare their ontology version; mixed-version indexes are the bug factory this prevents.
mechanism: Semantic versioning for the ontology; deprecation period before removal; migration maps per release; index metadata records the build version. Breaking changes bump major.
algo: O(changes) migration. The discipline is deprecate-then-remove, never silent deletion.

title: Curation workflows
description: Automated extraction proposes; humans dispose — curation workflows route candidate concepts and relations to domain experts for approval. The workflow tracks provenance (extracted from where, by which method), confidence, and reviewer decisions; approved items enter the ontology, rejected ones train the extractor. Throughput comes from good ranking (review the likely-correct first) and batch interfaces.
mechanism: Candidates with confidence + provenance -> review queue ranked by confidence -> approve/reject/edit -> feedback to the extractor. SLAs per queue; expert time is the bottleneck to optimize.
algo: O(candidates) review; ranking by confidence maximizes expert throughput.
demo:
candidates = [
    ('quantum_battery', 'IS-A', 'battery', 0.92, 'papers/2024'),
    ('flux_capacitor', 'IS-A', 'battery', 0.31, 'forums'),
]
print('REVIEW QUEUE (ranked by confidence):')
for term, rel, parent, conf, prov in sorted(candidates, key=lambda c: -c[3]):
    print('  [ ] %-16s %s %s (conf=%.2f, src=%s)' % (term, rel, parent, conf, prov))
print('approve -> ontology; reject -> trains the extractor')
print('automation proposes, humans dispose: rank so experts see the best first')

title: Evaluating ontologies
description: Ontology quality is measured against tasks, not aesthetics: does query expansion improve search recall? Do the concepts match how users talk (term coverage on real queries)? Metrics: coverage (% of query terms in the ontology), precision of relations (sampled expert review), and task lift (search metrics with/without expansion). An ontology nobody measures is decoration.
mechanism: Coverage on query logs; sampled precision review; A/B on the downstream task. Track per-release; regressions block the release.
algo: O(sample) review + O(queries) coverage. The downstream task is the ground truth.
demo:
# task-based eval: does expansion improve search?
queries = ['pup', 'auto', 'laptop']
onto_terms = {'pup', 'dog', 'auto', 'car'}  # ontology vocabulary

covered = [q for q in queries if q in onto_terms or True]  # expansion covers via relations
# simulated: recall with and without expansion
results = {'without': 0.62, 'with': 0.81}
print('query term coverage: %d/%d' % (sum(1 for q in queries if q in onto_terms), len(queries)))
print('search recall without expansion: %.2f' % results['without'])
print('search recall with expansion   : %.2f' % results['with'])
print('the downstream task decides: measure, don\'t admire')

title: Multilingual ontologies
description: Concepts are language-independent; labels are not: the concept 'dog' has labels in 300 languages, and the relations hold across all of them. Multilingual ontologies separate the concept node from its labels, so 'Hund' and 'dog' resolve to the same node. The hard parts are lexical gaps (no word for it in language X) and culture-specific concepts that do not translate.
mechanism: Concept nodes with per-language label sets; relations on concepts, not labels. Lexical gaps marked explicitly (no forced translation). Culture-specific concepts scoped to their locale.
algo: O(concepts * languages) labels; relations O(concepts). Gaps explicit, not papered over.

title: Domain ontologies
description: Domain ontologies go deep where general ones go wide: MeSH for medicine (30k descriptors), FIBO for finance, gene ontologies for biology. They encode the domain's actual conceptual structure — the relations experts use — and they are built with the experts, not for them. The payoff is precision: a medical search over MeSH beats keyword search by miles because the concepts match the domain's thinking.
mechanism: Expert-driven concept modeling; corpus-driven term extraction; alignment to upper ontologies where useful. Maintenance by the domain community (MeSH updates annually).
algo: O(domain concepts); expert time dominates. Annual update cycles.

title: Ontology reasoning
description: Reasoners derive what the ontology implies but never stated: if Dog IS-A Mammal and Mammal IS-A Animal, then Dog IS-A Animal (transitive closure). OWL reasoners also check consistency (no concept that is both A and not-A) and classify new concepts under the right parents. Reasoning runs at build time — materialize the inferences into the index — so queries stay fast.
mechanism: Transitive closure over IS-A; consistency checking via tableau/EL algorithms; classification of new concepts. Materialize inferences offline; query the closed graph.
algo: EL reasoning is polynomial; full OWL is exponential — choose the profile that fits. Materialize at build.

title: Keeping ontologies honest
description: Ontologies rot: stale concepts, contradictory relations, orphaned terms nobody uses. Honesty practices: provenance on every relation (where did this come from?), usage tracking (which concepts do queries actually touch?), deprecation for the unused, and consistency checks in CI. An ontology with 40% unused concepts is a museum; pruning is curation, not destruction.
mechanism: Provenance per relation; query-log coverage per concept; CI consistency checks; deprecation workflow for the unused. Review the bottom decile yearly.
algo: O(concepts) audits; the work is the review, not the computation.
